title: In-Place Reversal, Shifting, and Rotation
summary: Rearranging an array's contents without a second array: two-pointer reversal, why naive shifting is O(n·k), and three approaches to rotation by k with very different space costs.

slides.markdown:
**In-place** means rearranging an array's existing contents using only a constant amount of extra memory — no second array, no copy of the whole input. It's a constraint interviewers add on purpose, because it rules out the laziest correct answer and forces you to reason about actual element movement.

This topic covers three closely related in-place moves: reversing an array end to end, shifting it by k positions, and rotating it by k — the last of which has three genuinely different implementations with different space costs, and picking the right one is the actual skill being tested.

slides.subTitle: Swap from both ends toward the middle
slides.markdown:
The classic in-place reversal uses two pointers: one at index 0, one at index n-1. Swap the elements they point to, then move the left pointer right and the right pointer left, one step each. Stop when they meet or cross.

```python
def reverse(arr):
    left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while left < right:
        arr[left], arr[right] = arr[right], arr[left]
        left += 1
        right -= 1
```

Each element is touched exactly once (as part of exactly one swap), so this is O(n) time. No second array is allocated — just two index variables — so it's O(1) extra space. This two-pointer, converging-from-both-ends shape reappears constantly across array and string problems.

slides.subTitle: O(n·k), one step at a time
slides.markdown:
Shifting an array by k means moving every element k positions (left or right), dropping elements that fall off one end. The naive approach shifts by 1 repeatedly, k times: `for _ in range(k): shift_by_one(arr)`.

Each single-step shift touches every element once, so it's O(n). Doing that k times gives **O(n·k)** total — for k close to n, that's effectively O(n²).

The fix is the same idea as string-building with a buffer: don't repeat a full O(n) pass k times. Compute the final position of each element directly and move it there once — which is exactly what the rotation techniques below do.

slides.sectionTitle: Three ways to rotate by k
slides.markdown:
"Rotate the array right by k" (last k elements move to the front, everything else shifts right) has three standard solutions with very different space costs:

| Approach | Time | Space | Idea |
|---|---|---|---|
| Extra array | O(n) | O(n) | Write each element directly to its rotated index in a new array, then copy back |
| Block-swap juggling (cyclic replacement) | O(n) | O(1) | Move each element directly to its final position, following cycles |
| Reversal trick | O(n) | O(1) | Three reversals: whole array, then each half |

All three are O(n) time. Only the last two satisfy an "in-place, O(1) space" constraint — the extra-array version is the one candidates reach for first and the one interviewers usually disallow.

slides.subTitle: Reverse the whole array, then reverse each half
slides.markdown:
To rotate `[1,2,3,4,5,6,7]` right by k=3: reverse the whole array to get `[7,6,5,4,3,2,1]`, then reverse the first k elements (`[5,6,7,4,3,2,1]`), then reverse the remaining n-k elements (`[5,6,7,1,2,3,4]`) — which is exactly the correct rotation.

Why it works: a full reversal puts every element in reverse order, which is "almost" the rotated order except each of the two segments is itself backwards. Reversing each segment individually un-reverses just that segment, landing everything in its correct rotated position.

slides.sectionTitle: Rotating in O(n) time, O(1) space
slides.markdown:
```python
def reverse_range(arr, i, j):
    while i < j:
        arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]
        i += 1
        j -= 1

def rotate_right(arr, k):
    n = len(arr)
    k %= n                       # critical — see the pitfall below
    reverse_range(arr, 0, n - 1)
    reverse_range(arr, 0, k - 1)
    reverse_range(arr, k, n - 1)
```

Three reversal passes, each O(n), so the whole rotation is O(n) time — and every reversal reuses the same `arr`, so it's O(1) extra space. This reuses the exact two-pointer reversal from earlier in this topic three times over.

slides.subTitle: Moving each element directly to its final position
slides.markdown:
The alternative O(1)-space technique moves each element directly to its rotated destination, following the cycle it belongs to, instead of reversing.

Rotating right by k sends the element at index i to index `(i + k) % n`. Start at index 0, hold its value, move the element currently at its destination out first (saving it), drop the held value in, and repeat — following the chain until you return to the starting index, completing one **cycle**.

If that first cycle doesn't cover every index (which happens whenever `gcd(n, k) > 1`), start a new cycle from the next uncovered index and repeat. Every element moves exactly once across all cycles combined, so the whole operation is O(n) time, O(1) space — same bounds as the reversal trick, different mechanism.

Both hit O(n) time and O(1) space, so the choice between them is about clarity and edge cases, not asymptotics:

- **Reversal trick** — three simple, independent passes; easy to explain, easy to get right under pressure, easy to unit-test each reversal separately. The default choice in an interview.
- **Cyclic replacement** — one pass overall, potentially fewer total writes, but correctness depends on correctly handling multiple cycles when `gcd(n, k) > 1`, which is easy to get subtly wrong live.

A strong answer states both exist and picks the reversal trick unless asked specifically to minimize writes — naming cyclic replacement as the alternative signals you know the full solution space, not just one memorized trick.

Rotating an array of length n by k is identical to rotating it by `k % n` — rotating by n brings every element back to where it started. Skip the modulo and a caller passing k = 17 against a 5-element array either crashes on an out-of-range slice or silently does far more work than necessary walking through redundant full rotations.

Always compute `k = k % n` (and handle `n == 0` separately to avoid a divide-by-zero) before any reversal, swap, or cycle-following logic runs. It's one line, and every rotation implementation above depends on it being correct first.

A common failure in interviews: writing `rotated = arr[k:] + arr[:k]` (or the equivalent slicing in another language) and calling it in-place because it's one line and reuses the variable name `arr`. It isn't — slicing builds two new lists and concatenating them builds a third, all full copies of the input. That's O(n) space, exactly what the constraint was meant to rule out.

The tell in code review: any solution containing a full-size temporary — a new list, a copied slice, a `.copy()` — has failed the O(1) space requirement even if the final assignment overwrites the original variable. "In-place" means the *algorithm's peak extra memory* is O(1), not that the result ends up back in the same variable name.

slides.subTitle: The nuance that trips up the formula
slides.markdown:
"Rotate right by k" and "rotate left by k" are mirror operations, and it's easy to derive the wrong destination formula under pressure if you don't fix a direction first.

- **Rotate left by k:** element at index i moves to `(i - k + n) % n`; equivalently, the array behaves as if indexed starting from k.
- **Rotate right by k:** element at index i moves to `(i + k) % n`.

A left rotation by k is identical to a right rotation by `n - k` — useful for reusing one implementation for both directions instead of writing two. The reversal-trick recipe simply swaps which segment gets reversed first: for a left rotation, reverse the first k elements, then the rest, then the whole array (the mirror image of the right-rotation recipe from earlier).

Stating the direction convention explicitly before coding — "I'll treat rotate-right as moving the last k elements to the front" — avoids an off-by-direction bug that's easy to introduce silently.

slides.subTitle: The production-level catch
slides.markdown:
A staff-level catch that pure algorithm practice doesn't surface: mutating an array in place is only safe if nothing else holds a reference to it expecting the original contents.

If the array was passed in by reference (the default in Python, Java, JavaScript for lists/arrays/objects) and the caller — or another thread, or a cached view — still expects to read the pre-rotation data, an in-place rotation silently corrupts it out from under them. This is a real production bug class: a function that rotates "its" array in place when that array is actually a shared buffer, a memoized result, or a slice view backed by the same memory as a larger structure.

The practical rule: in-place mutation is a valid optimization only when you either own the array exclusively or have made an explicit contract with callers that the input will be modified. When in doubt, or when the array is shared, copy once (O(n) space) rather than chase an O(1)-space win that breaks correctness elsewhere.
